263: **[SECTION 6 --- BANK SET-OFF RIGHTS]{.underline}**
264: 
265: **[6.1 --- Pinnacle\'s Preferred Position (Green)]{.underline}**
266: 
267: Pinnacle\'s form ACA requires full subordination of the bank\'s liens and set-off rights in the controlled accounts to the Secured Party\'s security interest. The form language provides:
268: 
269: > *\"The Bank hereby subordinates all liens, security interests, encumbrances, claims, counterclaims, and rights of set-off that the Bank may now or hereafter have in or with respect to the Accounts and the funds on deposit therein to the security interest of the Secured Party.\"*
270: 
271: The rationale for this provision is straightforward: Pinnacle\'s security interest in the controlled accounts should be first-priority. If the bank can exercise set-off rights against controlled account balances --- for example, to satisfy unpaid loan obligations, treasury management fees, or other amounts owed by the Depositor to the bank --- Pinnacle\'s collateral can be diminished without notice to or consent of Pinnacle, potentially at the very moment when the borrower is in financial distress and the collateral is most needed to support Pinnacle\'s recovery. Full subordination eliminates this risk by ensuring that the bank\'s claims are junior to Pinnacle\'s security interest in all circumstances.
272: 
273: The priority rule of UCC § 9-327 reinforces Pinnacle\'s position: under § 9-327(1), a security interest held by a secured party that has control of a deposit account has priority over a conflicting security interest held by a secured party that does not have control. However, under § 9-327(3), a security interest held by the depository bank itself has priority over a security interest held by another secured party, even if the other secured party has control. This means that absent a contractual subordination, the bank\'s own security interest in the deposit account --- which arises by operation of the bank\'s relationship with the depositor --- would have priority over Pinnacle\'s security interest. The subordination provision in the ACA is designed to contractually override this statutory priority rule by requiring the bank to subordinate its claims. UCC § 9-339 permits such subordination by agreement.
274: 
275: **[6.2 --- Common Bank Pushback]{.underline}**
276: 
277: Banks virtually always resist full subordination of their set-off rights. The negotiation of the set-off provision is typically one of the most contentious aspects of ACA negotiation and often consumes a disproportionate share of the negotiation timeline. Common bank positions include:
278: 
279: > • **Preservation of Set-Off for All Depositor Obligations.** The bank seeks to preserve its right of set-off for \"any obligation owed to the Bank by the Depositor, whether direct or contingent, now existing or hereafter arising.\" This formulation is maximally broad and would permit the bank to set off against controlled account balances for obligations arising under credit facilities, loan agreements, letter of credit reimbursement obligations, treasury management agreements, and any other banking relationship between the bank and the Depositor --- including contingent or unliquidated obligations.
280: >
281: > • **Lookback Cap.** Some banks offer a compromise in which the bank\'s set-off is subordinated, but only with respect to obligations arising within a specified lookback period preceding the bank\'s receipt of a NOEC. For example, the bank might agree that its set-off rights are subordinated with respect to obligations that arose within the 90-day period prior to the NOEC, but that set-off for obligations arising prior to that 90-day period is preserved. The practical effect of a short lookback period is that the bank retains set-off for long-standing obligations --- such as a term loan that has been outstanding for several years --- while subordinating only recent or newly arising claims.
282: >
283: > • **Carve-Out for Bank Service Charges.** Banks frequently seek to carve out their customary service charges, maintenance fees, and per-item fees from the subordination, on the ground that these are de minimis amounts directly attributable to the operation of the controlled accounts.
284: 
285: In the current Ironbridge matter, the bank\'s Turn 1 markup proposes a 90-day lookback cap and preserves set-off for obligations \"whether direct or contingent.\" This position is significantly less protective than Pinnacle\'s preferred position and would leave Pinnacle exposed to the risk that the bank could set off against controlled deposit balances for obligations that predate the 90-day lookback period.
286: 
287: **[6.3 --- Acceptable Fallback Positions (Yellow)]{.underline}**
288: 
289: Three pre-authorized fallback positions are available for this issue, presented in order of preference:
290: 
291: **Fallback A --- Capped Lookback with Minimum Period.** Accept a lookback limitation, but insist on a minimum lookback of 180 days (i.e., the bank\'s set-off is subordinated with respect to obligations arising within the 180-day period prior to the bank\'s receipt of a NOEC). This 180-day minimum is the floor pre-authorized by the deal team and is based on the assessment that a 180-day lookback provides reasonable protection against preferential set-off in a distressed scenario while accommodating the bank\'s interest in preserving set-off for obligations that significantly predate the triggering event.
292: 
293: *Negotiation note:* Open with full subordination in the first counter-markup (the Green position). If the bank rejects full subordination, offer a 365-day lookback in the second counter-markup. Settle at no less than 180 days. Do not move below 180 days without escalation.
294: 
295: **Fallback B --- Carve-Out for Ordinary Course Bank Fees Only.** Accept a limited carve-out from subordination for the bank\'s customary and documented account maintenance fees, service charges, and per-item fees directly attributable to the operation of the controlled accounts, but exclude from the carve-out any amounts arising under credit facilities, loans, treasury management agreements for unrelated services, or any contingent obligations. The following sample language may be offered:
296: 
297: > *\"The subordination set forth herein shall not apply to the Bank\'s right to debit the Accounts for the Bank\'s customary and documented account maintenance fees and per-item charges directly attributable to the Accounts, in each case in amounts not exceeding those set forth in the Bank\'s fee schedule delivered to the Secured Party as of the date hereof.\"*
298: 
299: Key drafting points: (i) the carve-out is limited to fees \"directly attributable to the Accounts\" --- it does not extend to fees for unrelated banking services; (ii) the fee amounts must be \"documented\" and must not exceed the amounts set forth in the bank\'s fee schedule delivered to Pinnacle, which provides Pinnacle with visibility into the scope of the carve-out; and (iii) the carve-out operates as a narrow exception to an otherwise comprehensive subordination --- the subordination itself must remain in full force and effect for all other obligations.
300: 
301: **Fallback C --- Scope Limitation.** If the bank insists on preserving set-off rights beyond the ordinary-course fee carve-out, narrow the scope of the preserved set-off to exclude \"contingent\" obligations. The bank\'s set-off right should be limited to liquidated, due, and payable obligations of the Depositor to the bank, not contingent, disputed, or unliquidated claims. The following counter-language may be offered:
302: 
303: > *\"The Bank may exercise its right of set-off only with respect to obligations of the Depositor to the Bank that are then due and payable (and not contingent, disputed, or unliquidated) and that arise directly under deposit account agreements between the Bank and the Depositor relating to the Accounts.\"*
304: 
305: This scope limitation ensures that the bank cannot exercise set-off for speculative or contingent claims --- such as indemnification obligations that have not been reduced to judgment, guaranty obligations that have not been called, or swap termination amounts that have not been calculated --- and limits set-off to concrete, liquidated obligations arising directly from the deposit account relationship.
306: 
307: Fallback C may be combined with Fallback A (lookback cap) and Fallback B (ordinary-course fee carve-out) to create a composite position: the bank\'s set-off is subordinated subject to a 180-day lookback, limited to liquidated obligations arising under the deposit account agreements, with a narrow carve-out for ordinary-course fees.
308: 
309: **[6.4 --- Walk-Away / Escalation Triggers (Red)]{.underline}**
310: 
311: > • Any lookback period shorter than 180 days requires escalation to Diana Whitford. A lookback of less than 180 days significantly increases the risk that the bank could exercise set-off for pre-existing obligations during a period of borrower distress, reducing the controlled deposit balances available to Pinnacle as collateral.
312: >
313: > • Any set-off right that encompasses obligations arising under credit facilities, loan agreements, or other banking relationships unrelated to the controlled deposit accounts --- **escalate**. If the Depositor has a separate borrowing relationship with the bank, the bank\'s set-off for those obligations should be addressed in the intercreditor context, not through the ACA.
314: >
315: > • Any set-off right that operates after delivery of a NOEC (i.e., the bank can set off against controlled accounts even after Pinnacle has asserted exclusive control) --- **hard stop** unless limited to the narrow ordinary-course bank fee carve-out described in Fallback B above. Post-NOEC set-off for any material amount would effectively allow the bank to withdraw collateral from Pinnacle\'s exclusive control, defeating the purpose of the NOEC.
316: 
317: **[SECTION 7 --- BANK LIEN SUBORDINATION]{.underline}**
318: 
319: **[7.1 --- Pinnacle\'s Preferred Position (Green)]{.underline}**
320: 
321: Pinnacle\'s preferred position is full subordination of all bank liens, security interests, and rights of recoupment in the controlled accounts and all funds on deposit therein. The form ACA includes both (i) a subordination provision --- pursuant to which the bank expressly subordinates its liens and security interests to the security interest of the Secured Party --- and (ii) a disclaimer by the bank of any security interest, lien, or right of set-off except as expressly preserved in the ACA. The combination of these two provisions is designed to ensure comprehensive coverage: the subordination provision addresses liens that the bank acknowledges, while the disclaimer addresses liens that the bank may not have identified or may not be aware of.
322: 
323: **[7.2 --- Relationship to Set-Off Rights (Section 6)]{.underline}**
324: 
325: The bank lien subordination issue is closely related to, but distinct from, the set-off rights issue addressed in Section 6 of this playbook. Both issues are frequently addressed in the same ACA provision (or in adjacent provisions), and many bank markups conflate the two. However, the issues involve distinct legal concepts:
326: 
327: > • **Lien subordination** addresses the priority of competing property interests in the controlled deposit accounts. The bank may hold a security interest in the deposit accounts granted under a master banking agreement, a general pledge agreement, or a treasury management agreement. Lien subordination requires the bank to agree that its security interest is junior to Pinnacle\'s security interest, such that in any distribution or realization event, Pinnacle\'s claim is satisfied before the bank\'s claim.
328: >
329: > • **Set-off rights** address the bank\'s contractual or common-law right to apply account balances against the Depositor\'s obligations to the bank. Set-off is not a lien in the traditional sense but operates functionally as a self-help remedy that allows the bank to reduce account balances by the amount of the Depositor\'s indebtedness. UCC § 9-340 specifically preserves the effectiveness of a bank\'s right of set-off against a deposit account, even if the bank does not hold a security interest in the account.
330: 
331: Both issues must be addressed in the ACA. A bank markup that subordinates the bank\'s \"lien\" but preserves an unrestricted set-off right is functionally ineffective, because the bank can achieve the same result through set-off that it would achieve through enforcement of a senior lien. Conversely, a provision that limits set-off but does not subordinate the bank\'s lien leaves Pinnacle\'s priority position unresolved. The negotiator should ensure that any agreed language covers both concepts comprehensively and consistently.
332: 
333: **[7.3 --- Acceptable Fallback Positions (Yellow)]{.underline}**
334: 
335: The same fallback framework described in Section 6 of this playbook applies to both set-off rights and lien subordination. The lookback cap (Fallback A), scope limitation (Fallback C), and ordinary-course fee carve-out (Fallback B) described in Section 6.3 should be applied consistently across both the lien subordination and set-off provisions.
336: 
337: An additional issue arises in the lien subordination context that does not arise in the set-off context: if the bank has a security interest in the deposit accounts granted under a separate agreement --- such as a master banking agreement, a treasury management agreement, or a general business loan agreement between the bank and the Depositor --- the ACA must expressly address that pre-existing lien. Pinnacle\'s form ACA includes a representation by the bank that no such prior liens exist; however, if the bank deletes this representation (as Ironbridge has done in its current Turn 1 markup), the negotiator should take the following steps:
338: 
339: > **(i)** Request that the bank identify and provide a schedule of any existing liens, security interests, or rights of set-off that the bank holds with respect to the controlled accounts, including the agreement under which each such lien was granted and the obligations secured thereby.
340: >
341: > **(ii)** Negotiate the express subordination of each identified pre-existing lien in the body of the ACA. The subordination should be specific --- identifying the agreement under which the lien was granted and the nature of the secured obligations --- rather than generic.
342: >
343: > **(iii)** If the bank refuses to subordinate a pre-existing lien, escalate immediately in accordance with the Red-tier triggers below.
344: 
345: **[7.4 --- Walk-Away / Escalation Triggers (Red)]{.underline}**
346: 
347: All escalation triggers and hard stops described in Section 6.4 apply with equal force to the bank lien subordination issue. Additionally:
348: 
349: > • If the bank discloses a pre-existing lien that it refuses to subordinate, **escalate immediately** to Diana Whitford and Thomas Orr. An unsubordinated prior bank lien could defeat Pinnacle\'s priority under UCC § 9-327(3), which gives the depository bank\'s security interest priority over the security interest of a non-bank secured party that has control. The subordination agreement in the ACA is the mechanism by which Pinnacle contractually overrides this statutory priority rule; without it, Pinnacle\'s security interest is junior as a matter of law.
350: >
351: > • If the bank refuses to provide a schedule of existing liens when requested, escalate. The refusal to disclose pre-existing liens suggests that the bank may hold liens that it is unwilling to subordinate, and Pinnacle should not execute the ACA without clarity on this issue.
352: 
353: **[SECTION 8 --- INDEMNIFICATION AND LIABILITY]{.underline}**
354: 
355: **[8.1 --- Pinnacle\'s Preferred Position (Green)]{.underline}**
356: 
357: Pinnacle\'s form ACA includes the following indemnification and liability framework:
358: 
359: > • **Depositor Indemnification of the Bank.** The Depositor (borrower) indemnifies and holds harmless the bank from and against all claims, losses, liabilities, costs, and expenses arising out of or relating to the ACA. This provision is standard and generally uncontroversial; it is expected by all depository banks and should not be the subject of significant negotiation.
360: >
361: > • **Secured Party Indemnification of the Bank.** The scope of the Secured Party\'s indemnification obligation is limited to losses arising from the Secured Party\'s own willful misconduct. This narrow scope reflects Pinnacle\'s position that the Secured Party should not bear the risk of losses arising from the bank\'s performance of its own obligations under the ACA, the Depositor\'s actions, or any other cause unrelated to the Secured Party\'s intentional wrongdoing.
362: >
363: > • **No Liability Cap.** The form ACA does not include an aggregate cap on the bank\'s liability. The bank\'s liability for breach of its obligations under the ACA is unlimited.
364: >
365: > • **No Consequential Damages Waiver.** The form ACA does not include a waiver of consequential, indirect, or punitive damages. All categories of damages are available to Pinnacle in the event of a bank breach.
366: 
367: **[8.2 --- Common Bank Pushback: Indemnification Scope]{.underline}**
368: 
369: Banks routinely seek to expand the scope of the Secured Party\'s indemnification obligation to cover losses arising from the bank\'s compliance with Pinnacle\'s instructions, including losses resulting from the bank\'s own negligence --- and, in aggressive markups, even losses resulting from the bank\'s gross negligence. The bank\'s position is that it is acting as a ministerial agent in complying with the Secured Party\'s instructions and should be held harmless for any adverse consequences of doing so.
370: 
371: In the Ironbridge Turn 1 markup, Section 6 of the ACA includes indemnification coverage for the bank\'s gross negligence. Specifically, the bank\'s markup provides that the Secured Party and the Depositor shall indemnify the bank for all losses \"arising out of or relating to the Bank\'s compliance with instructions of the Secured Party, regardless of the Bank\'s negligence or gross negligence.\" This formulation is unacceptable.
372: 
373: **Client Directive:** Coverage for the bank\'s gross negligence must be rejected. Pinnacle will not indemnify the bank for losses that result from the bank\'s own gross negligence, willful misconduct, or bad faith. This is a firm position that reflects both sound risk management and established market practice. The vast majority of ACAs executed in the leveraged lending market include a gross-negligence carve-out from the bank\'s indemnification, and Pinnacle should not agree to a formulation that falls below this market standard.
374: 
375: The indemnification should cover the bank only for losses arising from (i) the Secured Party\'s instructions that the bank follows in good faith, and (ii) the bank\'s performance of its obligations under the ACA, in each case except to the extent arising from the bank\'s own gross negligence, willful misconduct, or bad faith. The following sample counter-language reflects the acceptable indemnification provision:
376: 
377: > *\"The Depositor and the Secured Party, jointly and severally, shall indemnify and hold harmless the Bank and its officers, directors, employees, and agents from and against any and all claims, losses, liabilities, costs, and expenses (including reasonable attorneys\' fees) arising out of or relating to the Bank\'s performance of its obligations under this Agreement or the Bank\'s compliance with instructions delivered by the Secured Party hereunder; provided, however, that the foregoing indemnification shall not extend to any claims, losses, liabilities, costs, or expenses to the extent arising from the Bank\'s own gross negligence, willful misconduct, or bad faith.\"*
378: 
379: Note the use of \"to the extent\" language in the carve-out, which provides for allocation of liability in mixed-fault scenarios (i.e., where the loss results in part from the bank\'s gross negligence and in part from other causes). This language is preferable to a formulation that eliminates the indemnification entirely if the bank\'s gross negligence contributed to the loss in any degree, because it preserves the bank\'s indemnification for the portion of the loss not attributable to its own misconduct.
380: 
381: **[8.3 --- Common Bank Pushback: Aggregate Liability Cap]{.underline}**
382: 
383: Banks frequently insert an aggregate cap on the bank\'s liability under the ACA, limiting the bank\'s total exposure for all claims --- whether arising from breach of contract, negligence, breach of fiduciary duty, or any other theory --- to a fixed dollar amount. The cap is typically set at a level that bears little or no relationship to the value of the controlled deposit balances.
384: 
385: In the current Ironbridge matter, the bank has proposed a \$50,000 aggregate liability cap in Section 7(a) of the bank\'s Turn 1 markup. This cap is wholly inadequate. The total controlled deposit balances in the Graycliff/Ironbridge transaction are approximately \$38,150,000 across three accounts (●●●●-4471, ●●●●-4472, and ●●●●-4473). A \$50,000 cap would limit the bank\'s liability to approximately 0.13% of the assets at risk --- a de minimis amount that would provide no meaningful deterrent against bank error and no meaningful recovery in the event of a bank breach that results in the loss of controlled funds.
386: 
387: **Client Directive:** The \$50,000 cap must be deleted entirely, or, if a cap is unavoidable to close the negotiation, it must be tied to the aggregate balances in the controlled accounts at the time of the loss-producing event, thereby ensuring that the cap is meaningful relative to the assets at risk.
388: 
389: **Acceptable Fallback:** If a cap is required to close the negotiation, offer a cap equal to the lesser of (a) the aggregate balance in all controlled accounts as of the date of the act, omission, or event giving rise to the claim, and (b) a fixed dollar amount equal to the facility size (here, \$175,000,000). This formulation ensures that the cap reflects the actual risk exposure --- the value of the collateral that the bank is charged with controlling --- rather than an arbitrary fixed amount. The following sample counter-language should be used:
390: 
391: > *\"The Bank\'s aggregate liability under this Agreement shall not exceed the aggregate balance of the Accounts as of the date of the act, omission, or event giving rise to such liability.\"*
392: 
393: **Negotiation Tactic:** Present the deletion of the cap as Pinnacle\'s primary position. If deletion is rejected, offer the balance-based cap as a fallback, framing it as a commercially reasonable alternative that protects both parties: the bank\'s exposure is limited to the value of the assets it controls (no more, no less), and Pinnacle retains meaningful recourse in the event of a bank breach.
394: 
395: **[8.4 --- Common Bank Pushback: Consequential Damages Waiver]{.underline}**
396: 
397: Banks routinely seek a mutual waiver of consequential, indirect, special, punitive, and exemplary damages. In the current Ironbridge markup (Section 7(b)), the bank has proposed a mutual waiver. This is a standard commercial provision that appears in many banking agreements and is not inherently objectionable, provided it is drafted correctly.
398: 
399: **Pinnacle\'s Position:** A mutual waiver is acceptable provided it satisfies the following conditions:
400: 
401: > **(i)** The waiver must be truly mutual --- i.e., both the Secured Party and the bank waive consequential damages. A waiver that runs only in the bank\'s favor (i.e., only the Secured Party waives consequential damages, but the bank does not) is unacceptable.
402: >
403: > **(ii)** The waiver must not carve out the bank\'s right to seek consequential damages in connection with the indemnification obligations. The indemnification provision (Section 8.2 above) is a contractual risk-allocation mechanism, and the consequential damages waiver should not override it.
404: >
405: > **(iii)** The waiver must not inadvertently limit Pinnacle\'s right to recover direct damages equal to the full account balances. In a scenario where the bank breaches the ACA by releasing controlled funds to the Depositor after receiving a NOEC, the amount of the released funds constitutes direct damages --- not consequential damages --- and should not be subject to the waiver.
406: 
407: The following language is acceptable:
408: 
409: > *\"No party hereto shall be liable to any other party for any indirect, consequential, special, punitive, or exemplary damages arising out of or relating to this Agreement, regardless of the form of action or theory of liability; provided that this Section shall not limit the obligations of the Depositor or the Secured Party under Section \[Indemnification Section\].\"*
410: 
411: **Escalation Trigger:** If the bank\'s proposed waiver is not mutual --- i.e., only the Secured Party waives consequential damages, but the bank does not --- reject outright and escalate to Diana Whitford. A non-mutual waiver is commercially unreasonable and creates an asymmetric risk allocation that favors the bank at Pinnacle\'s expense.
412: 
413: **[8.5 --- Walk-Away / Escalation Triggers (Red)]{.underline}**
414: 
415: > • Bank indemnification covering gross negligence --- **must be rejected**; no fallback is available. This is a firm client directive. The gross-negligence carve-out is a minimum protection that Pinnacle requires in all ACAs.
416: >
417: > • Aggregate liability cap below the lesser of aggregate account balances and \$5,000,000 --- **escalate to Diana Whitford**. A cap below \$5,000,000 is presumptively inadequate in any transaction where controlled deposit balances exceed \$10,000,000.
418: >
419: > • Non-mutual consequential damages waiver --- **escalate** to Diana Whitford. While a mutual waiver is acceptable, a one-sided waiver that benefits only the bank is not.
420: >
421: > • Any indemnification provision requiring Pinnacle to indemnify the bank for the bank\'s compliance with instructions that the bank knows or should know are unauthorized or fraudulent --- **hard stop**. The bank cannot outsource its own anti-fraud and due-diligence obligations to the Secured Party through the indemnification provision.
422: 
423: **[SECTION 9 --- GOVERNING LAW]{.underline}**
424: 
425: **[9.1 --- Pinnacle\'s Preferred Position (Green)]{.underline}**
426: 
427: Pinnacle\'s form ACA is governed by the laws of the State of New York, without regard to conflict of laws principles. This governing-law selection reflects several considerations:
428: 
429: > • New York has well-developed UCC jurisprudence, particularly with respect to Article 9 perfection and control issues. New York courts have addressed numerous disputes involving deposit account control agreements, priority contests under UCC § 9-327, and the requirements for \"control\" under UCC § 9-104, providing a mature body of case law that reduces interpretive uncertainty.
430: >
431: > • Pinnacle and Hargrave Stein & Collier LLP are based in New York, and the negotiating team\'s familiarity with New York law enables more efficient evaluation of legal issues arising under the ACA.
432: >
433: > • The Credit Agreement in most Pinnacle transactions is governed by New York law, and the other Loan Documents (security agreements, pledge agreements, guaranty agreements, intercreditor agreements) are typically also governed by New York law. Selecting New York law for the ACA creates consistency across the transaction documents and avoids the complexity that arises when different documents in the same transaction are governed by different states\' laws.
434: >
435: > • New York\'s conflict of laws rules, if applicable, could potentially lead to the application of another state\'s law under a \"most significant relationship\" or \"center of gravity\" analysis; the exclusion of conflict of laws principles ensures that New York law applies regardless of the location of the deposit accounts or the bank.
436: 
437: **[9.2 --- Common Bank Pushback]{.underline}**
438: 
439: Depository banks frequently insist on the governing law of the bank\'s home jurisdiction --- i.e., the state in which the bank is headquartered or chartered. For example, Ironbridge National Bank, N.A. is headquartered in Charlotte, North Carolina and is chartered under OCC Charter No. 18742 as a national banking association. In the current Ironbridge matter, the bank\'s Turn 1 markup substitutes North Carolina governing law for New York governing law.
440: 
441: Banks typically cite their standard form requirements and internal compliance policies as the basis for insisting on home-state governing law. Bank counsel may also argue that the controlled accounts are maintained in the bank\'s home state and that the law of the state in which the accounts are maintained should govern. Some banks have rigid internal policies that prohibit execution of ACAs under any governing law other than the bank\'s home-state law, and these policies may be difficult to overcome through negotiation.
442: 
443: **[9.3 --- Acceptable Fallback Positions (Yellow)]{.underline}**
444: 
445: **Fallback A --- New York Remains Strongly Preferred.** Push back firmly on governing-law changes; New York governing law should be achieved in the majority of Pinnacle\'s transactions. Present the consistency argument: the Credit Agreement is governed by New York law; all other Loan Documents are governed by New York law; the ACA should be consistent with the balance of the transaction documents to avoid choice-of-law complexity and potential interpretive inconsistencies.
446: 
447: If the bank raises the location-of-accounts argument, note that UCC § 9-304 governs the choice-of-law rules for perfection of security interests in deposit accounts and that the law of the bank\'s jurisdiction determines perfection and priority --- but this does not require the ACA\'s contractual governing law to match. The ACA\'s governing law determines the interpretation and enforceability of the contractual provisions; UCC § 9-304 independently determines the law governing perfection and priority.
448: 
449: **Fallback B --- Concession if Deal-Breaker.** If the bank identifies governing law as a genuine deal-breaker --- i.e., the bank will not execute the ACA under New York law under any circumstances, and the governing-law issue is the sole remaining impediment to closing --- this provision may be conceded. Diana Whitford has indicated that governing law is not a hill to die on if it is the last open issue in the ACA negotiation.
450: 
451: If conceding on governing law, the negotiator should take the following steps before accepting the bank\'s proposed jurisdiction:
452: 
453: > **(i)** Confirm that the chosen law (e.g., North Carolina) does not produce a materially different result on any critical UCC issue relevant to the ACA, including the requirements for \"control\" under § 9-104, the perfection requirements under § 9-312(b)(1), the priority rules under § 9-327, and the effectiveness of set-off under § 9-340. For states that have adopted the Uniform Commercial Code without material non-uniform amendments to Articles 8 and 9 --- which includes the substantial majority of U.S. jurisdictions --- the governing-law choice is generally not outcome-determinative on these critical issues.
454: >
455: > **(ii)** Conduct a brief choice-of-law analysis to identify any non-uniform amendments adopted by the bank\'s home state. North Carolina has adopted the Uniform Commercial Code substantially as promulgated, without material non-uniform amendments to Articles 8 or 9 that would affect the ACA analysis. Accordingly, concession of North Carolina governing law in the current Ironbridge matter would not be expected to produce a materially different legal result.
456: >
457: > **(iii)** Insert a severability clause (if not already present) and a UCC § 9-304 acknowledgment, if applicable, to ensure that the governing-law selection does not inadvertently alter the choice-of-law rules for perfection and priority.
458: 
459: **[9.4 --- Walk-Away / Escalation Triggers (Red)]{.underline}**
460: 
461: > • If the bank proposes the law of a jurisdiction that has adopted non-uniform amendments to UCC Article 9 affecting deposit account control --- currently an unusual scenario, but one that should be monitored --- **escalate to Thomas Orr** for a full choice-of-law analysis before conceding. Non-uniform amendments could alter the requirements for \"control\" under § 9-104, the priority rules under § 9-327, or the effectiveness of the bank\'s waiver of set-off rights, and the implications must be fully understood before Pinnacle agrees to such a governing-law selection.
462: >
463: > • If the bank proposes arbitration in lieu of court jurisdiction --- **reject**. Pinnacle requires court jurisdiction (preferably the state or federal courts sitting in New York, or, if governing law has been conceded to the bank\'s home state, the courts of the bank\'s home state). Arbitration is inappropriate for ACA disputes because (i) Pinnacle may need injunctive relief (e.g., an order compelling the bank to comply with a NOEC), which is more readily available from a court than from an arbitral tribunal, and (ii) arbitration proceedings are typically slower and more expensive than summary court proceedings for the types of disputes likely to arise under an ACA. Jury trial waivers, by contrast, are standard and acceptable.
464: 
465: **[SECTION 10 --- TERMINATION]{.underline}**
466: 
467: **[10.1 --- Pinnacle\'s Preferred Position (Green)]{.underline}**
468: 
469: Pinnacle\'s form ACA provides that the ACA may be terminated only in one of two ways:
470: 
471: > **(i)** By written agreement of all three parties (the Secured Party, the Depositor, and the bank); or
472: >
473: > **(ii)** Upon written notice from Pinnacle (the Secured Party) to the bank, delivered when the obligations under the Credit Agreement have been indefeasibly paid in full and the security interest in the controlled accounts has been released in accordance with the terms of the Loan Documents.
474: 
475: Under the form ACA, the bank has no unilateral right to terminate. The rationale is fundamental: if the bank can unilaterally terminate the ACA, Pinnacle loses control of the deposit accounts, and its perfection --- which depends entirely on the ACA --- is destroyed. A bank with a unilateral termination right holds the power to extinguish Pinnacle\'s security interest at will, which is an unacceptable structural vulnerability in Pinnacle\'s collateral package.
476: 
477: **[10.2 --- Common Bank Pushback]{.underline}**
478: 
479: Banks routinely seek a unilateral termination right, typically on 30 days\' written notice to the Secured Party and the Depositor. In the current Ironbridge matter, the bank\'s Turn 1 markup proposes a 30-day unilateral termination right (Section 10 of the bank\'s form).
480: 
481: The bank\'s rationale for a unilateral termination right typically includes the following arguments:
482: 
483: > • The bank needs the ability to exit the ACA if its relationship with the Depositor deteriorates --- for example, if the Depositor\'s account activity presents Bank Secrecy Act / Anti-Money Laundering compliance concerns, if the Depositor becomes the subject of a law enforcement investigation, or if the Depositor engages in account activity that violates the bank\'s acceptable use policies.
484: >
485: > • The bank needs the ability to exit the ACA if its internal policies change --- for example, if the bank decides to exit a particular line of business, to close certain account types, or to discontinue its institutional deposit services platform.
486: >
487: > • The bank needs the ability to terminate the ACA if the Depositor fails to pay the bank\'s maintenance fees or other charges.
488: >
489: > • The bank is not a party to the Credit Agreement and should not be indefinitely bound by a tripartite agreement that it cannot exit.
490: 
491: These arguments have varying degrees of merit, but none justifies a short-notice unilateral termination right without protective conditions for the Secured Party. The negotiation should focus on extending the notice period and imposing conditions on the effectiveness of termination to ensure that Pinnacle has adequate time and opportunity to establish replacement accounts and obtain a replacement ACA before the bank\'s termination becomes effective.
492: 
493: **[10.3 --- Acceptable Fallback Positions (Yellow)]{.underline}**
494: 
495: **Fallback A --- Extended Notice Period with Transition Rights.** If the bank will not accept elimination of its unilateral termination right (which is the preferred outcome), insist on a minimum notice period of ninety (90) days (rather than the bank\'s proposed 30 days), coupled with the following protective conditions:
496: 
497: > **(i)** During the notice period, the bank shall continue to comply with all of its obligations under the ACA, including any Notice of Exclusive Control then in effect. Termination of the ACA does not relieve the bank of its obligation to honor an outstanding NOEC during the notice period.
498: >
499: > **(ii)** The Depositor shall use commercially reasonable efforts to establish replacement deposit accounts at a depository bank reasonably acceptable to the Secured Party and to deliver to the Secured Party a replacement Account Control Agreement covering such replacement accounts, in form and substance reasonably satisfactory to the Secured Party, prior to the expiration of the notice period.
500: >
501: > **(iii)** The ACA shall not terminate until the Secured Party has confirmed in writing to the bank that a replacement Account Control Agreement has been executed and delivered.
502: 
503: The following sample language incorporates all three conditions:
504: 
505: > *\"The Bank may terminate this Agreement upon not less than ninety (90) days\' prior written notice to the Secured Party and the Depositor; provided that (i) during such notice period, the Bank shall continue to comply with all of its obligations hereunder, including any Notice of Exclusive Control then in effect, (ii) the Depositor shall use commercially reasonable efforts to establish replacement deposit accounts at a depository bank reasonably acceptable to the Secured Party and to deliver to the Secured Party a replacement Account Control Agreement covering such replacement accounts, in form and substance reasonably satisfactory to the Secured Party, prior to the expiration of such notice period, and (iii) this Agreement shall not terminate until the Secured Party has confirmed in writing to the Bank that a replacement Account Control Agreement has been executed and delivered.\"*
506: 
507: Condition (iii) is the critical element of this fallback. By making the effectiveness of the bank\'s termination contingent on Pinnacle\'s written confirmation that a replacement ACA is in place, this formulation ensures that there is no gap in Pinnacle\'s perfection. The bank initiates the termination process by delivering notice, but the termination does not take effect until the Secured Party is satisfied that its collateral protection has been replicated at a successor institution.
508: 
509: **Fallback B --- Termination Conditioned on Replacement ACA (Shorter Notice Period).** If the bank will not accept a 90-day notice period, seek a termination mechanic conditioned on the Secured Party\'s written confirmation that a replacement ACA has been executed and delivered, even with a shorter notice period (e.g., 30 or 60 days). Under this formulation, the bank may initiate termination on 30 or 60 days\' notice, but termination does not become effective until the Secured Party confirms in writing that a replacement ACA is in place. This is the strongest protective formulation short of eliminating the unilateral right entirely, because it prevents any gap in perfection regardless of the length of the notice period.
510: 
511: In practical terms, the difference between Fallback A and Fallback B is the length of the notice period --- 90 days vs. 30 or 60 days. The replacement-ACA condition (condition (iii) in Fallback A) is the essential protective element in both fallbacks. If the bank accepts the replacement-ACA condition, the length of the notice period is secondary; conversely, if the bank rejects the replacement-ACA condition, a longer notice period provides Pinnacle with more time to arrange a replacement but does not guarantee perfection continuity.
512: 
513: **[10.4 --- Walk-Away / Escalation Triggers (Red)]{.underline}**
514: 
515: > • Unilateral bank termination on fewer than 90 days\' notice without a replacement-ACA condition --- **escalate to Diana Whitford**. Depending on the specific bank and transaction context, this may be acceptable if other protective conditions are present (e.g., continued NOEC compliance during the notice period), but the deal team must make this determination on a case-by-case basis.
516: >
517: > • Unilateral bank termination that takes effect automatically upon expiration of the notice period regardless of whether a replacement ACA is in place --- **hard stop** unless the notice period is at least 180 days. A termination that takes effect automatically --- without any confirmation from the Secured Party and without regard to whether replacement arrangements have been made --- creates an unacceptable gap risk. With a 180-day notice period, Pinnacle has sufficient time to identify a successor bank, negotiate a replacement ACA, and arrange for the transfer of accounts; with a shorter period, the risk of a perfection gap is material.
518: >
519: > • Any termination provision that also terminates the bank\'s obligation to comply with an outstanding NOEC during the notice period --- **hard stop**. This scenario is particularly dangerous: if the bank can both terminate the ACA *and* cease complying with an outstanding NOEC during the notice period, Pinnacle could lose both contractual control and operational control of the deposit accounts simultaneously, allowing the Depositor to withdraw funds during a post-default period when Pinnacle needs exclusive control most urgently.
520: 
521: **[SECTION 11 --- SUCCESSOR-BANK OBLIGATIONS]{.underline}**
522: 
523: **[11.1 --- Pinnacle\'s Preferred Position (Green)]{.underline}**
524: 
525: Pinnacle\'s form ACA requires the bank to provide written notice to the Secured Party not fewer than thirty (30) days prior to any of the following events:
526: 
527: > **(i)** Any transfer, assignment, or novation of the bank\'s rights or obligations under the ACA to a successor bank;
528: >
529: > **(ii)** Any transfer of the controlled accounts to a successor bank in connection with a merger, acquisition, consolidation, or reorganization of the bank; or
530: >
531: > **(iii)** Any change of the bank\'s name, charter, or organizational identity.
532: 
533: The form further provides that any successor bank shall be bound by the terms of the ACA and that the bank shall not transfer the controlled accounts to a successor unless the successor bank has executed a written agreement assuming the bank\'s obligations under the ACA. This assumption requirement ensures that there is no gap in the ACA\'s coverage: the successor bank steps into the shoes of the original bank and is contractually bound to comply with Pinnacle\'s instructions (including any outstanding NOEC) on the same terms.
534: 
535: **[11.2 --- Common Bank Pushback]{.underline}**
536: 
537: Banks frequently delete successor-bank notification and assumption requirements entirely, citing the following concerns:
538: 
539: > • In certain bank transactions --- particularly FDIC-assisted acquisitions, OCC-mandated conservatorships, and Purchase and Assumption agreements --- the assuming bank inherits the failed bank\'s deposit liabilities by operation of law. The assuming bank typically has no pre-closing relationship with the depositors or their secured parties and cannot be required to execute assumption agreements in advance of a transaction that may occur on an expedited basis (sometimes over a single weekend).
540: >
541: > • The bank may be prohibited by confidentiality obligations or securities laws from disclosing a pending merger or acquisition prior to its public announcement.
542: >
543: > • The bank\'s internal policies may prohibit the execution of agreements that purport to bind future successors without the successor\'s independent consent.
544: 
545: In the current Ironbridge matter, the bank\'s Turn 1 markup deleted the successor-bank notification obligation in its entirety, leaving the ACA silent on the question of what happens if Ironbridge is acquired by, merged with, or succeeded by another institution.
546: 
547: **[11.3 --- Acceptable Fallback Positions (Yellow)]{.underline}**
548: 
549: **Fallback A --- Notification Only (Delete Assumption Requirement).** Accept deletion of the requirement that a successor bank execute an assumption agreement in advance, but retain the notification obligation. The bank must notify Pinnacle promptly --- and in any event within five (5) business days --- after the bank becomes aware of any proposed or pending merger, acquisition, transfer of accounts, or change of charter that would result in a successor bank holding the controlled accounts. This gives Pinnacle time to evaluate whether a new ACA is required with the successor institution and to take appropriate action (including contacting the successor\'s counsel, preparing a draft ACA, and coordinating with the Depositor\'s counsel) before the transition occurs.
550: 
551: **Fallback B --- Commercially Reasonable Efforts.** If the bank refuses even a notification obligation --- which is a more aggressive position and relatively unusual --- require the bank to use \"commercially reasonable efforts\" to notify the Secured Party of any successor-bank event and to cooperate with the Secured Party in obtaining a replacement ACA from the successor bank. This is a soft obligation but ensures that the bank is not entirely silent on the successor-bank question. A commercially-reasonable-efforts standard is generally enforceable and, at a minimum, requires the bank to take such steps as a reasonable commercial actor would take under the circumstances, even if it does not guarantee a specific result.
552: 
553: **Fallback C --- Assignment Provision.** Insert a general non-assignment clause providing that the bank shall not assign or transfer its rights or obligations under the ACA without the Secured Party\'s prior written consent (which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed); provided that the bank may assign its rights and obligations to a successor in connection with a merger, consolidation, or acquisition without the Secured Party\'s consent, but shall promptly notify the Secured Party of such assignment. This formulation gives Pinnacle a consent right over voluntary assignments (e.g., the bank\'s decision to transfer the Depositor\'s accounts to an affiliate) while acknowledging the practical reality that the bank cannot obtain Pinnacle\'s consent for an involuntary or regulatory-driven succession (e.g., an FDIC-assisted acquisition).
554: 
555: **[11.4 --- Walk-Away / Escalation Triggers (Red)]{.underline}**
556: 
557: > • Complete deletion of both the notification obligation and any successor-bank language --- **escalate to Diana Whitford**. While this is not a hard stop --- perfection survives a bank merger by operation of UCC § 9-315 and related provisions, and the ACA\'s obligations generally transfer to a successor by operation of law in a merger --- it creates significant operational risk because Pinnacle may lose visibility into its bank counterparty. If the bank is acquired by an institution that does not recognize the ACA or that takes the position that the ACA did not survive the merger, Pinnacle could face a dispute over control of the deposit accounts at precisely the moment when it needs to exercise that control.
558: >
559: > • If the bank refuses all fallback positions and insists on a fully silent ACA regarding successors, escalate for a risk assessment tied to the specific bank\'s likelihood of merger or acquisition activity. For a large, stable national bank, the risk may be manageable; for a smaller community bank or a bank that has been the subject of regulatory action, the risk may be unacceptable.
560: 
561: **[SECTION 12 --- REPRESENTATIONS AND WARRANTIES]{.underline}**
562: 
563: **[12.1 --- Pinnacle\'s Preferred Position (Green)]{.underline}**
564: 
565: Pinnacle\'s form ACA includes the following representations and warranties by the bank:
566: 
567: > **(a) No Prior Control Agreement.** The bank has not entered into, and will not enter into, any agreement with any other person pursuant to which the bank has agreed, or will agree, to comply with instructions or entitlement orders concerning the Accounts originated by such other person. This is the single most important bank representation in the ACA: if the bank has entered into a competing control agreement, the holder of that agreement may have priority over Pinnacle\'s security interest under UCC § 9-327 (which awards priority to the first secured party to obtain control).
568: >
569: > **(b) No Known Claims.** The bank does not know of any claim to or interest in the Accounts, other than the security interest of the Secured Party and the Depositor\'s rights as account holder. This representation provides Pinnacle with a contractual basis for a claim if a third party subsequently asserts an interest in the Accounts that the bank knew about at the time of execution.
570: >
571: > **(c) Account Renaming Notice.** The bank will not change the name or account number of any Account without thirty (30) days\' prior written notice to the Secured Party. A change in account number could affect the enforceability of the ACA if the ACA identifies the Accounts by number (which it typically does), and prior notice enables Pinnacle to amend the ACA or update its records accordingly.
572: >
573: > **(d) Account Location.** The Accounts are maintained at the office of the bank set forth in the notice provisions of the ACA. The location of the Accounts may be relevant for UCC choice-of-law purposes under § 9-304.
574: >
575: > **(e) Bank Status.** The bank is a \"bank\" within the meaning of UCC § 9-102(a)(8). This representation confirms that the depository institution satisfies the UCC\'s definition of a \"bank\" and that the ACA is therefore effective to confer \"control\" over a \"deposit account\" as those terms are used in Article 9.
576: 
577: **[12.2 --- Common Bank Pushback]{.underline}**
578: 
579: The most frequently resisted representation is **(a)** --- the \"no prior control agreement\" representation. Banks resist this representation for several reasons:
580: 
581: > • The bank may not want to represent that it has conducted a comprehensive internal search of all agreements affecting the Accounts. In a large institution with multiple divisions and legacy systems, confirming the absence of a prior control agreement may require significant internal coordination.
582: >
583: > • The bank may have other agreements that it views as potentially conflicting with the representation --- for example, garnishment compliance obligations, tax levy procedures, or blocked account agreements entered into in connection with other banking relationships --- even though these agreements may not technically constitute \"control agreements\" under the UCC.
584: >
585: > • Bank counsel may take the position that the representation exposes the bank to liability if a competing agreement is subsequently discovered, and that the bank should not bear this risk.

587: In the Ironbridge Turn 1 markup, the bank deleted representation (a) in its entirety. Representation (c) (account renaming) was modified to reduce the notice period from thirty days to ten days and to add a carve-out for changes required by law or regulatory order.
